title: Motivation — no, it’s not 90% of learning, but it does matter to an extent
author: Daniel Muijs
summary: Daniel Muijs synthesizes recent meta-analyses and longitudinal studies on the relationship between motivation and academic attainment, cutting through the popular claim that 'motivation is 90% of learning.' The research reveals two key complications: 'motivation' is defined inconsistently across studies (as intrinsic drive, self-efficacy, mastery orientation, mindset, and more), making comparisons difficult. Effect sizes are modest: in Howard et al.'s (2021) large meta-analysis, intrinsic motivation correlated with attainment at .11 and identified motivation at .13, while a-motivation correlated negatively at .21. Most importantly, the causal direction runs more strongly from attainment to motivation than the reverse: Vu et al.'s (2024) longitudinal meta-analysis found that attainment's effect on motivation was nearly twice as strong as motivation's effect on attainment. The exception is self-belief, which had a significant bidirectional impact on achievement—stronger than any other motivational construct. The practical takeaway: motivation strategies are worth using, but strategies that directly enhance attainment and competence are more important, since success itself is the most reliable motivator.
points: 'Motivation' refers to many different constructs across studies (intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, mastery orientation, mindset beliefs)—a definitional inconsistency that muddles cross-study comparisons and inflates popular claims about its importance.

Effect sizes between motivation and attainment are modest across meta-analyses (.11–.32 depending on how motivation is defined), and the causal arrow runs nearly twice as strongly from attainment to motivation as from motivation to attainment.

Self-belief is the motivational construct with the strongest and most consistent relationship to attainment—and the only one with a significant bidirectional effect—making it a more promising intervention target than general 'motivation boosting.'
quotes: motivation refers to a lot of different-but-related things in different studies, which is unfortunately very common in educational research.

Generally relationships were quite weak, with a-motivation negatively correlated with attainment (effect size .21, this is usually classified as modest), and intrinsic and identified motivation positively correlated with it
Vu et al (2024) found that the effect of attainment on motivation was nearly twice as strong as the effect of motivation on attainment, though both were significant.

This is what we find in most longitudinal studies: a reciprocal effect, i.e. attainment and motivation influence each other, but one in which the effect of attainment on motivation is stronger than the other way round

while motivation does affect attainment, the effect is modest. And the effect of attainment on motivation is stronger than vice versa. In practice this means that yes, it is worth using strategies that improve motivation in the classroom, but it is more important to use strategies that enhance attainment, learning and competence in students.
